Hydrogen is stored, compressed, and dispensed at high pressures, so infrastructure components such as compression, storage, and purification systems must be integrated (DOE HFTO 2025a). Hydrogen fuels also have different hazard properties than petroleum fuels (e.g., a greater flammability range and faster combustion), which impact siting and storage (Hydrogen Tools 2025). Hydrogen’s high flammability poses a risk of accidental fires or explosions due to its low ignition energy and propensity to leak, although safer hydrogen storage technologies are being developed to mitigate these risks (Balcerzak, Lau, and Heubner 2024; Bhuiyan and Siddique 2025). In a military setting, the site selection for storage must consider proximity to munitions, other fuel storage areas, housing, and training facilities. Allowing sufficient time and budget for full operational testing and broad intra-DOW sharing of lessons learned would mitigate potential safety risks. 3.3 Changing Workforce Needs The integration and maintenance of expanded energy technologies necessitate specialized advanced training for DOW employees or contractors responsible for managing these systems. Frequent reassignment of active-duty personnel often results in staff exposure to a wide range of systems, fostering generalists rather than specialists. This can limit the development of deep expertise in any one area, potentially impairing the proper operations and maintenance of advanced energy technologies and leading to unforeseen costs and potential equipment breakdowns. The increased variety of advanced energy technologies compounds this problem, potentially creating gaps in institutional knowledge and slowing the effective deployment and maintenance of expanded energy technologies across installations. Changes in defense contracts create challenges for retaining skilled workers within defense supply chains, and once these workers leave, they become difficult and expensive to rehire and retrain or replace (DOD 2022). Competition for skilled talent related to advanced energy technologies is expected to intensify in the coming years, suggesting worker shortages and increased labor costs for DOW energy needs. For example, in the United States, there is a projected shortage of 1 million electricians by 2030. An underdeveloped solar training pipeline and the absence of recognized apprenticeship programs has left 97% of PV companies struggling to find qualified workers, and labor costs 8 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. increased 25% in 2023, with further labor market tightening expected as the PV market expands (Huckstep and Dempster 2024). Access to experienced cybersecurity professionals with energy expertise to defend advanced energy systems could pose the greatest challenge, and the DOD Cyber Workforce Strategy 2023–2027 flagged the shortage of skilled professionals as a continuing risk to operational readiness and national security. In 2024, there were 500,000 unfilled vacancies for experienced cybersecurity personnel in the United States, while DOW reported a shortfall of 28,000 military and civilian cyber professionals (House Committee on Homeland Security 2024; Pomerleau 2024).
